claims.text: The baseline material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA thin film sputtered directly onto a standard substrate.
A 10–20 nm high-thermal-conductivity interlayer beneath a 100 nm HEA film is the controlled intervention.
Copper or monolayer graphene can serve as the proposed high-thermal-conductivity interlayer.
The interlayer will form a well-adhered, continuous interface.
The interlayer will facilitate rapid interfacial heat transfer.
The interlayer will modify the residual-stress state at the HEA/interlayer interface.
Enhanced heat dissipation during rapid magnetic-cooling cycles will reduce local temperature gradients and thermal lag.
Reduced thermal lag will lessen kinetic impediments to magnetic-domain reorientation.
Reduced kinetic impediments to domain reorientation will decrease domain-wall pinning.
Decreased domain-wall pinning will reduce magnetic hysteresis.
Improved thermal management will produce a sharper magnetocaloric response that more closely resembles intrinsic bulk behavior.
Interlayer-bearing films will thermally equilibrate faster than baseline films during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Interlayer-bearing films will have narrower hysteresis loops than baseline films.
Interlayer-bearing films will exhibit an enhanced peak magnetic entropy change at low applied field.
The predicted improvements will persist at higher cycling frequencies.
The hypothesis applies to approximately 100 nm films under low applied fields when heat-transfer kinetics are limiting.
Interfacial roughness or interdiffusion may alter magnetic anisotropy and the magnitude of the predicted improvement.
VSM hysteresis measurements and Kerr microscopy can respectively characterize hysteresis loops and magnetic-domain dynamics.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies a 10–20 nm interlayer while giving monolayer graphene as an example; a graphene monolayer is far thinner than 10–20 nm.
